originalRequest: Author a complete English course for the open Agent-courses site on agent tools and MCP, slug learn-agent-tools-mcp, for a developer who wants an agent to reach real systems — their data, APIs, internal services. Terminal task: connect to, or minimally implement, an MCP server and complete one real tool call with an explicit permission boundary. Six lessons covering tools versus skills, the client/server model, what the current specification's core guarantees, how a tool's description determines whether it gets called correctly, long-running work, and permission boundaries with injection risk. Recency is a hard rule: establish the current specification version from the specification's own site before writing anything, and teach mechanism and judgment rather than any product's click-path.
learnerBrief: A developer who already runs a coding agent on real work and has hit the wall where the agent cannot reach the systems the work is about. They paste query results, log lines, and ticket bodies into chat by hand. They can read JSON and run terminal commands, and they can follow short annotated Python, but they have not read a protocol specification and have no working model of what sits between their agent and an external system. They need enough of the protocol to make good decisions — not an SDK walkthrough that will be wrong in three months.

briefCompleteness.evidence: The request specified the audience ('a developer who wants an agent to reach real systems — their data, APIs, internal services'), the terminal task ('connect to, or minimally implement, an MCP server and complete one real tool call with an explicit permission boundary'), the lesson count and the six themes, and two explicit scope boundaries: draw the line against agent-skills-reuse in Lesson 1 then stay out of Skill territory, and leave repository instruction files to agent-readable-repo. It also constrained the treatment — teach mechanism and judgment, not an SDK tutorial that will rot. That is a starting point, an objective, and constraints, so it is not a bare topic name.
briefCompleteness.assumptionsMade: Two judgment calls were made from evidence rather than asked. First, the reader's Python level: the request permits code 'only where it illustrates a durable mechanism', and the one code example retained (an SDK deriving a tool definition from a docstring) is short, annotated, and stamped with the documentation date it was read from — so a reader who does not write Python can still follow the mechanism. Second, the choice to make lesson 6's grid an explicitly declared synthesis rather than dropping it: the underlying requirements are all cited, and the lesson text states in the body that the arrangement is the course's own.

learnerModel.targetReader: A developer who can already operate a coding agent on real tasks and is currently acting as the manual transport between that agent and their own systems.
knownConcepts: Running a coding agent on a multi-step task and reading its output
Running commands in a terminal and reading an error message
HTTP request/response, status codes, and the idea of a header
What an API and an API token are, and that a token grants access
Reading a short annotated Python function well enough to follow what it declares
unknownConcepts: MCP itself — the protocol, its primitives, and its architecture
JSON-RPC message shapes and error code conventions
OAuth flows, scopes, and audience validation beyond 'a token grants access'
Any specific MCP SDK's classes, decorators, or package layout
Writing or operating a production server of any kind
The internals of how a host application assembles a model request
learnerModel.assumedEnvironment: The reader has their own agent client, a terminal, and at least one system they already have credentials for — a database, an issue tracker, an internal API. The course assumes no particular client, no cloud account, no MCP server already connected, and no ability to install anything privileged. It never asks the reader to upload data or paste a credential anywhere.
learnerModel.firstIndependentAction: After Lesson 1, sort three moments from their own recent agent sessions where they were the manual transport into Skill-shaped, server-shaped, both, or neither — using only the who-does-the-work test taught in that lesson, with no tool installed and nothing connected.
noviceRamp: The bridge from known to unknown starts at an experience the reader already has — pasting query results into chat — and names it as a reach problem before any protocol vocabulary appears. MCP is introduced only after the reader has sorted their own examples into the two piles.

The architecture is taught as a four-participant trace of one request before any wire format is shown, so the reader has a mental picture to hang `tools/call` on rather than meeting the method name first.

Every term follows the everyday-handle-then-formal-name order: 'a connector the host creates' before 'client', 'text you did not write' before 'untrusted content', 'a durable handle instead of blocking' before 'task'.

The one code block in the course is annotated line by line for what it demonstrates rather than for how to write it, and is explicitly marked as illustrating a durable mechanism whose specific API names will change.

Every exercise points at the reader's own environment and states where to run the command, what success looks like, and what to record on failure. The Level 1 exercises in Lessons 1 and 2 need nothing installed, so a reader with no server connected still has real work to do.

Both halves of the terminal task are reachable: a reader who can connect an existing server does that, and a reader who prefers to write one is told explicitly that 'small' means one read-only tool over one operation.

scope: Covers the boundary between a Skill and an external capability; the host/client/server architecture and what server isolation does and does not guarantee; what the 2026-07-28 protocol revision's stateless core requires, what every request must carry, and where cross-request state moved; tool definitions as an interface the model reads at decision time, including the two error channels; long-running work through the Tasks extension and the extension-versus-core boundary that governs its availability; and the permission boundary around a tool call, including the four channels through which text the reader did not write reaches the model. Deliberately excludes: writing Agent Skills (its own course), repository instruction files (its own course), any SDK walkthrough beyond one illustrative snippet, OAuth flow implementation, MCP Apps and the UI extensions, resources and prompts beyond naming them, server hosting and operations, and any client's UI click-path.

evidence: The specification's own versioning page, read 2026-08-23, states in one sentence that 'The current protocol version is 2026-07-28' — this was the first research action of the session, before any lesson content was planned.

The 2026-07-28 changelog, read 2026-08-23, independently confirms the revision and enumerates its breaking changes: removal of the initialize handshake and protocol-level sessions, the mandatory server/discover RPC, and the move of Tasks into the io.modelcontextprotocol/tasks extension.

The MCP blog's release post for this revision (published 2026-07-28) frames it as 'MCP's most important since remote MCP first launched over a year ago' and describes the core as transforming 'into a request/response stateless protocol'.

The blog index and RSS feed, read 2026-08-23, show the most recent posts as 'The 2026-07-28 Specification' (2026-07-28) and 'The New MCP Roadmap' (2026-08-22) — no newer specification release exists as of the check date.

The roadmap post published 2026-08-22, one day before authoring, names the priorities expected to move next: transport unification, agentic messaging, agent identity, result handling, and tool catalog discovery.
topicCurrency.staleRisk: This is the most version-exposed course in the library and it will age unevenly. Ages first, within one revision: everything in Lesson 3 — the required _meta keys, the error codes, server/discover's mandatory status, and the statement that 2026-07-28 is current. A reader should re-check the versioning page before trusting any of it, which Lesson 3 tells them to do and Lesson 6 repeats as a closing habit. Ages second: Lesson 5's Tasks material, because extensions 'evolve independently of the core protocol' and can change without a protocol revision — the extension identifier, the five lifecycle states, and the tasks/get and tasks/update method names are all extension surface. Ages third: the SDK snippet in Lesson 4, whose class name, decorator, and package are the single fastest-moving lines in the course; the lesson stamps it with the documentation date and says so explicitly. Ages fourth: the Claude Code specifics in Lesson 1 and Lesson 6 (the /mcp panel, the scope table, the approval status strings), which are one vendor's product surface. Ages fifth but should be read as already dated: the Zuplo survey figures, gathered mid-November to mid-December 2025, before this revision existed. Ages slowest: the architecture and isolation principles in Lesson 2, the description-craft guidance in Lesson 4, and the trust reasoning in Lesson 6, which have survived several revisions. The roadmap items in Lesson 6 are intent rather than shipped behaviour and nothing in the course rests on them.
topicCurrency.recheckProcedure: Open the specification's versioning page and read the sentence naming the current version. If it is still 2026-07-28, the course stands. If it is later, open that revision's changelog and diff it against Lesson 3's claims first, then Lesson 5's, then re-read the Tasks extension page independently of the core changelog.

qualitySelfReview.diagramUse: One mermaid sequence diagram, in Lesson 2, tracing a single tool call across you, model, host, client, server, and the target system. It earns its place because the lesson's central claim — that the model requests rather than makes a call, and that the host is the only component seeing both the conversation and the pending call — is a statement about ordering and position that costs a paragraph in prose and one glance as a diagram. It carries a sentence before it saying what to look for and three observations after it. No diagram was used in Lessons 1, 3, 4 or 6: Lesson 1's content is a two-column distinction better served by a table, Lesson 3's is normative rules rather than structure, Lesson 4's is a symptom-to-cause mapping already tabulated, and Lesson 6's grid is itself the visual. Lesson 5's lifecycle is a five-row table because the states are a set with terminal members, not a flow with branching. Lesson 2 also carries a hotspot interaction over a five-node diagram, which is a different job from the mermaid — it asks the reader to point at the consent boundary rather than to read a sequence.
weakestPoints: The outline came pre-set from the design brief — six lessons against six named themes — and was auto-confirmed in a non-interactive run. No human reviewed the lesson order, the coverage, or the depth before the prose was written. The DAG was checked mechanically and the load balanced (196-246 non-code lines per lesson, 6-7 new concepts each), but if the intended reader wanted, say, more on authorization and less on descriptions, nothing in this run would have caught that.

The terminal task cannot be verified by the author. Lesson 6 asks the reader to complete a real tool call against their own system behind a boundary they wrote, and the course has no way to check that it happened, that the boundary was written before rather than after, or that the reader read the connection dialog instead of clicking through. The exercise rubric asks which gate fired specifically to make a skipped boundary visible to the reader themselves, but that is self-report.

Lesson 6's two-by-two permission grid is a synthesis, not a rule from any source. It is declared as such in the lesson body, and each underlying requirement it composes is separately cited — human-in-the-loop, showing tool inputs, treating results as untrusted, scope minimization. But the specific arrangement into four cells with four different gates is the course's own invention and has not been validated against anyone's real deployment. A reader could follow it precisely and still have a bad boundary if their situation does not decompose along those two axes.

Lesson 5 teaches a mechanism many readers cannot use. Tasks are an extension, off by default, with optional SDK support and client support that the documentation itself says 'varies by client'. The lesson handles this by teaching the judgment (blocking versus handle versus task) and giving an explicit fallback design, but a reader whose client lacks the extension finishes the lesson with a well-understood mechanism and no way to run it.

The adoption evidence is thin and the course says so repeatedly, which is honest but leaves a real gap. The only builder-population figures are from one vendor's self-selected survey with no published sample size, gathered before the current revision existed. The partner quotes in the release post are vendor self-reports with no method. There is no independent measurement of MCP deployment in this course because none was found that met the sourcing bar, and a reader looking for 'how widely is this actually used' does not get an answer.

The two Anthropic engineering essays (2024-12-19 and 2025-09-11) carry a large share of Lesson 4. They are first-party, durable, and cited for design principles rather than mechanics — and the lesson states their dates and that limitation in the body. But a reader could reasonably want description guidance grounded in something newer than the protocol revision it is being applied to.
followUpChecks: Re-open the specification's versioning page. If the current revision is no longer 2026-07-28, diff the new changelog against Lesson 3 before anything else, then Lesson 5.
Re-run the Lesson 4 SDK snippet against the current build-server documentation — the class name, decorator, and package are the most likely lines in the course to be wrong first.

Have a reader who is not the author attempt the Lesson 6 terminal task and report which gate fired, to find out whether the six-step boundary procedure is actually followed in order or whether step 2 gets written retrospectively.
Look for an independent, methodologically stated measurement of MCP production deployment to replace or supplement the Zuplo figures, and drop the survey citation entirely if a better one exists.

Check whether the Tasks extension's lifecycle states or method names have changed independently of the core protocol, since extensions evolve on their own timeline and Lesson 5 would not be caught by a core-revision check.

acceptanceReview.scoreNotes: structure 5: all six lessons carry objectives, a lesson-specific hook heading, explanation, worked example, faded example, exercises and a distinct closing heading; the README lesson table and Prev/Next chain are complete and the DAG is clean. grounded 5: fifteen sources, every one opened during this session, with the current protocol revision established from the specification's own versioning page before any content was planned and cross-checked against the changelog and the release post; every volatile claim carries its revision or publication date, and the two older essays are flagged in the body text as pre-dating the current revision. pedagogy 4 rather than 5: the worked-to-faded-to-independent ladder holds in all six lessons, but Lessons 3 and 6 ask more of the reader than Lesson 1 does, and the terminal task's success depends on the reader having a system they can safely experiment against — which the course cannot supply. exercises 4: every exercise has approach guidance, measurable criteria, a reference answer and progressive hints, and three carry explicit common-mistake breakdowns; held at 4 because verification is entirely self-report in the reader's own environment. load 4: 6-7 new concepts per lesson against a cap of about 7, so the course sits at the top of its band rather than comfortably inside it; lesson lengths are balanced at 196-246 non-code lines with no outlier. readable 4: prose is chunked and the citations sit under the sentences they support, but Lesson 3 carries an unavoidable density of normative quotation, since paraphrasing a MUST NOT weakens it.
acceptanceReview.terminalTask: The reader connects an existing MCP server, or writes a minimal one exposing a single read-only tool, over a system they already have access to — then completes one real tool call from their own agent. Before connecting, they write a six-part permission boundary: what is connected and who wrote it, every tool marked on both axes of the grid, which tools run without asking, where untrusted text can enter, what they are relying on, and what the boundary does not cover. After the call they record the tool, the arguments, whether the arguments were what they expected, and which of their written gates actually fired — including recording that none fired, if none did.
acceptanceReview.interactionCheck: Five body interaction blocks across six lessons, one per lesson except Lesson 5 which carries an order block, plus three agentmentor-action cards. Lesson 1, agentmentor-check 'Choose between reading and calling': serves the misconception that a documented procedure implies a Skill, using a case where three of four steps need reach — the distractor most readers pick is the one that sorts by how procedural the task feels. Lesson 2, agentmentor-hotspot 'Point at the component that can refuse a call': five nodes, one correct, serving the two wrong beliefs that produce bad permission designs — that the model's restraint or the server's validation is the safety layer; each wrong node's feedback explains why that component structurally cannot hold the decision. Lesson 3, agentmentor-check 'Locate cross-call state under the current core': serves the specific staleness this course exists to correct, since both wrong answers people reach for (connection identity, session header) describe mechanisms this revision removed. Lesson 4, agentmentor-fix 'Rewrite a description the model keeps misreading': the reader edits a docstring against three local regex checks, each message explaining the mechanism rather than the rule; chosen over a check block because the misconception here is only visible when you try to write the fix. Lesson 5, agentmentor-order: six steps of a task lifecycle, serving the two most-misplaced items — capability declaration, which readers place as a setup step because it was one before this revision, and the approval, which readers resolve by re-issuing the original call. Lesson 6, agentmentor-check 'Judge which pairing needs a per-call gate': all four options are individually reasonable setups, so the block tests composition rather than tool assessment. The three action cards are lesson-specific training moves rather than generic buttons: a reasoning audit on the reader's own Lesson 1 sort, a mastery probe that surfaces which of the reader's beliefs came from pre-2026-07-28 sources, and a pressure scenario that kills the client at minute three of the reader's own long-running design. Lessons 2 and 4 carry no action card, to keep the density at roughly one interaction per lesson.
acceptanceReview.learnerFitCheck: Targets a developer who can operate a coding agent and read JSON but has never read a protocol specification — the person currently pasting query results into chat. Three hidden prerequisites were removed. First, no prior MCP vocabulary: the course opens on the reader's own pasting behaviour and does not name a protocol primitive until the reader has sorted their own examples. Second, no SDK or language requirement: the single Python snippet is annotated for the mechanism it demonstrates, not for how to write it, and the terminal task explicitly permits connecting an existing server instead of writing one. Third, no protocol-reading background: JSON-RPC shapes are introduced through a traced request rather than through the schema, and the wire-level examples appear only after the reader has a picture of who is talking to whom. The first independent action — sorting three of their own moments into Skill-shaped, server-shaped, both or neither — needs nothing installed and nothing connected, and depends only on Lesson 1's who-does-the-work test plus the reader's own memory of their week. Each subsequent lesson's exercise raises the environment requirement by one step: read your connected servers, audit one server's documentation, rewrite one description, classify your own long work, and finally make the call. A reader who has nothing connected can complete Lessons 1 through 4 against documentation alone.
promotionNotes: Before promotion to examples/, re-open the specification's versioning page and confirm 2026-07-28 is still current. If it is not, the course is not wrong but Lesson 3 needs a revision diff and the version stamps throughout need updating.
The Lesson 4 SDK snippet should be re-run against the live build-server documentation at promotion time rather than trusted from this session's cache.

The Lesson 6 permission grid is the course's own synthesis and is labelled as one. If it survives contact with several readers' real setups, consider whether it is worth proposing more widely; if readers' situations do not decompose along its two axes, that is a signal to rework it rather than defend it.
The Zuplo survey citation is the weakest source in the file and is presented with three explicit limits. Replace it if a measurement with a published method appears.
No temporary slug, no placeholder text, and every source URL was verified to return 200 without redirect at authoring time.
